chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr and Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, all from Umar ibn Udhaynah, who said:

I said to Zurarah: I heard Muhammad ibn Muslim and Bukayr narrating from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) regarding a case with a husband, parents, and one daughter: The husband gets one-fourth, which is three shares out of twelve; the parents get two-sixths, which is four shares out of twelve; and the remaining five shares belong to the daughter, because if she were a son, she would not have more than five out of twelve. And if there were two daughters, they get five out of twelve shares, because if they were two sons, they would not have more than the remaining five. Zurarah said: This is the truth if you want to apply 'awl (proportional reduction) so that the fixed shares do not exceed the whole. Indeed, the reduction enters only those who have the surplus from the children and the paternal and maternal sisters. As for the husband and the maternal siblings, they are not reduced from anything that Allah has specified.

key_terms.اَلرُّبُع: Ar-rub': One-fourth, a specific share for the husband.
key_terms.اَلسُّدُسَانِ: As-sudusani: Two-sixths, a specific share for the parents.
key_terms.اَلْأَخَوَات: Al-akhawat: Sisters, specifically referring to paternal and maternal sisters in this context.
key_terms.اَلْأَسْهُم: Al-ashhum: Shares, referring to the fractional portions of the estate.
key_terms.اَلْعَوْل: Awl: The proportional reduction of shares when the sum of fixed portions exceeds the total estate.

ai.seo_question: How are inheritance shares calculated when the total exceeds the estate in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Zurara validates the calculation method of 'Al-Wal' (proportional reduction) by Muhammad ibn Muslim, confirming that in cases where fixed shares exceed the estate, the reduction is applied to those with variable shares (children and sisters) rather than the fixed Quranic heirs like the husband. This hadith is pivotal in Shia jurisprudence for establishing that the husband's quarter share is immutable and not subject to the 'awl' mechanism, distinguishing him from other heirs whose portions are derived from the residue or variable fractions.
